answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: We believe consequential methods if developed in a standard way could help show the impact of Virtual Power Plants (collections of DERs acting in concert). However, when used inappropriately, we risk confusion, double counting or overstating impacts.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: The grid mix is changing quickly in many countries, so impacts will vary each year.

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text:
Behind-the-meter capacity (batteries, solar that is self consumed vs exported, Demand Side response) all have impacts on the grid. Currently we treat the changes they make in operating or build margin as zero. In other words, we do not account for them. In future when we have thousands of EVs and devices interacting, this will have consequences for grid operators, but today it is very difficult to measure this.

There isn’t a commonly agreed marginal emissions factor or methodology that is used, so we use average hourly emissions factors. If there were a marginal emissions factor agreed, we would be able to use it and show the impact of fleets of decentralised energy resources (DERs).

We currently can create ‘Energy Attribute Certificates’ for the impact of shifting demand from one hour to another, based on average emissions factors. These are closer to ‘efficiency certificates’ found in some markets than Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin (REGOs). If we are trying to build electrification and Virtual Power Plants that deliver demand side flexibility as fast as we want to build new generation, given the need to combine flexibility with variable generation, we need to think of the demand side more like the supply side.

These EACs act as the ‘flip’ side of the REGOs, helping tip the business case for individual, small-scale sites to adopt low carbon solutions. Sites can sell EACs to strengthen the business case for electrification (a bit like selling an I-REC based on self-consumption which is already part of the I-REC standard).

One solution to the complexity of the knowing the consequence (either build or operational) of each small scale device could be thresholds for load size – for instance, under 10 MW of DERs / VPP, use average emissions factors because we can’t attribute a direct cause and effect from one asset to its grid impact. For over 10 MW VPPs (when you know DERs have acted to flexibly avoid a power plant being used instead, perhaps using similar additionality tests such as open market data from the UK balancing mechanism), marginal factors could be used. The threshold could be different for each market or could be provided by a market operator.

answers.label: Research supporting the suggested approach
answers.text:
In a 2023 report by Arup, Energy Unlocked and Quantaco on 24/7 Carbon Free Energy London, we modelled a range of low carbon, distributed technologies and their impact on emissions.

Excerpt from the technical modelling report:
"Data scientists at Advanced Infrastructure provided us with an estimate of hourly marginal carbon intensity for 2030. Using this to measure the consequence of demand-side flexibility operation in our 2030 CFE flex scenarios, we observed a small net increase in consequential system emissions for both of the CFE flex scenarios, despite seeing reductions to emissions when considering the grid average carbon intensity. This analysis suggests that if all of London attempts to maximise their CFE score, there could be undesired emissions impacts.

This is an important issue to track as more buildings adopt a 24/7 CFE approach and it highlights the central importance of coordinating signals carefully and having transparency of data used for system control decisions. However, we believe it should not temper the short-term role of a 24/7 CFE approach as an incentive to drive forward flexibility deployment; consequential impacts will not be substantial until large scale up of the approach, while very significant uncertainty also exists over the future marginal intensity profile used in the analysis."
(detailed technical modelling results available on request)
